options.content:
**How to read this dashboard.** Charts count production code only, not tests, vendored or non-code files. Hover a title for what a chart measures and how to read it.
Change and entropy charts use the last 100 commits that touched code, read weekly; neighbouring points share most commits, and faint lines span two standard errors. A dashed line at 1 marks chance: module boundaries make no difference.
Dependency charts draw one line per language. A file's *reach* is the files it depends on through its imports and theirs.
No metric is validated against defects yet: read trends within this repository, not absolute values.

panels.title: Production code size
panels.description:
SIZE. What: production code at each commit, in tokens (value) and files; tests, vendored and non-code files excluded.

Read: context, not a score. A step marks a bulk commit, which often moves other charts too.

Trend: size is the strongest single predictor of defects: judge the other trends against it.

panels.title: Commits crossing modules (vs chance) ↓
panels.description:
CHANGES. What: how often files changed in the same commit sit in different modules, relative to chance, over the last 100 code commits each week. Lower is better.

Read: 1 means module boundaries make no difference to what changes together; below 1, modules change independently. Dashed lines span two standard errors.

Trend: rising means modules must change together more, through coupling no import shows. Change coupling correlates with defects.

panels.title: Rework within 7 days ↓
panels.description:
CHANGES. What: the share of edits to files already changed in the previous 7 days, over the last 100 code commits each week. Lower is better.

Read: 0.2 means a fifth of a typical commit's edits rework last week's code. Expect high values during feature work.

Trend: rising means code does not settle. A faster commit pace raises it too (see span_weeks). Unvalidated.

panels.title: File ownership by top author ↑
panels.description:
CHANGES. What: for files changed at least twice in the last 100 code commits, the share of changes made by their most active author, each week. Higher is better.

Read: 0.8 means a typical file's main author made 80% of its changes. Dashed lines span two standard errors.

Trend: falling means more people change code nobody owns, which went with more defects (Bird et al.). Squash merges credit the merger.

panels.title: Work spread: effective files
panels.description:
ENTROPY. What: over how many files the work of the last 100 code commits is effectively spread, each week; each commit counts once.

Read: 12 means as if spread evenly over 12 files. Files per commit is shown because bigger commits spread work by themselves.

Trend: rising means more places change at once. It predicted faults well in open-source projects (Hassan).

panels.title: Work spread: effective modules
panels.description:
ENTROPY. What: over how many modules the work of the last 100 code commits is effectively spread, each week.

Read: 3 means as if spread evenly over 3 modules; it cannot exceed the module count (right axis).

Trend: rising while the module count holds means work scatters; rising with it may only mean the code was split.

panels.title: Encapsulated code share ↑
panels.description:
STRUCTURE. What: the share of function code in non-public functions (no pub, static, not exported, leading underscore). Higher is better.

Read: 0.6 means 60% of function code is internal. Visibility is written differently per language: compare by_language over time.

Trend: falling means the public surface grows faster than the code behind it.

panels.title: Duplicated code share ↓
panels.description:
STRUCTURE. What: the share of function code (functions of 50+ tokens) whose structure occurs more than once, ignoring names and literals. Lower is better.

Read: 0.05 means 5% of it has a structural twin.

Trend: rising means copy-paste instead of reuse. Whole-function clones only. Unvalidated.

panels.title: Code in large functions ↓
panels.description:
STRUCTURE. What: the share of function code in functions over 200 tokens. Lower is better.

Read: 0.5 means half of it sits in large functions. Compare by_language over time.

Trend: rising means logic piles up in a few large functions. Unvalidated.

panels.title: Decision points per 100 tokens
panels.description:
COMPLEXITY. What: decision points (if, loops, match arms, catch, ternaries, &&, ||) per 100 production tokens.

Read: 5 means one decision every 20 tokens. Languages differ: compare by_language over time.

Trend: rising means more paths to understand and test per line. Unvalidated.

panels.title: Block nesting below function body
panels.description:
COMPLEXITY. What: how many blocks deep function code sits below the function body, weighted by tokens; deep_share is the code in functions nested more than 3 deep.

Read: 1.5 means typical code is one to two blocks deep. Else-if chains stay flat.

Trend: rising means more conditions to keep in mind while reading. Unvalidated.

panels.title: Global mutable state per 1,000 tokens
panels.description:
NONLOCAL. What: declarations of global mutable state per 1,000 production tokens: Rust static mut, C/C++ file-scope variables, Python global, JS/TS module-level let and var.

Read: the forms differ: compare by_language over time.

Trend: rising means behaviour depends on more state outside the code in view.

panels.title: Throws and panics per 1,000 tokens
panels.description:
NONLOCAL. What: non-local exits per 1,000 production tokens: throw, raise, Rust panics, unwrap and expect, C longjmp.

Read: in Rust mostly unwrap and expect; elsewhere throws a distant caller must handle. Compare by_language.

Trend: rising means control leaves functions in more places a caller cannot see. Unvalidated.

panels.title: goto per 1,000 C/C++ tokens
panels.description:
NONLOCAL. What: goto statements per 1,000 C/C++ tokens.

Read: mostly the goto-cleanup idiom, which is benign: watch spikes, not the level.

Trend: rising outside error cleanup means jumps that defeat top-to-bottom reading. Unvalidated.

panels.title: Share of its language's code a file depends on ↓
panels.description:
DEPENDENCIES. What: the share of the other files of its language that a typical production file depends on, through its imports and theirs (its reach), per language (c, rust, python, ecma). Lower is better.

Read: 0.1 means a file depends on a tenth of its language's code. mean_reach and median_reach count files; largest_cycle is the largest group of files importing each other.

Trend: rising means a change anywhere can affect, and requires understanding, more of the code (MacCormack et al.).

panels.title: Imports crossing modules (vs chance) ↓
panels.description:
DEPENDENCIES. What: how often imports cross module boundaries, relative to chance, per language (c, rust, python, ecma). Lower is better.

Read: 1 means modules make no difference to what imports what; below 1, files mostly import within their module.

Trend: rising means modules lean on each other more and stop matching the code's structure. Steps when modules are split or merged.

panels.title: How changed files rank by dependencies
panels.description:
DEPENDENCIES. What: how the files changed by commits rank among the files of their language by reach (the files they depend on), over the last 100 code commits each week.

Read: 50% means work lands on typical files; 70% means on files that depend on more than 70% of their peers do. Active files usually rank high: read the trend. reach is their mean reach in files.

Trend: rising means work concentrates on code that needs more context to change safely. Unvalidated.

panels.title: Imports resolved (coverage of the charts beside)
panels.description:
DEPENDENCIES. What: the share of imports naming this repository that resolve to a file, per language (c, rust, python, ecma). External code is left out.

Read: the dependency charts miss what this misses. fallback_share counts imports resolved only to a crate root or __init__.py, which overstates reach.

Trend: a drop means the dependency charts read too low, not that the code changed.
